meta.blurb: Every day at Eastgate market, good vegetables spoil in the heat. Ravi, a young engineer, wonders why nobody has fixed it. He sketches a cold box that runs on sunlight, and learns why one small market comes before a big one.
meta.bible: Ravi: a young engineer in his late twenties, thoughtful, stubborn and kind. Nadia: Ravi's friend, a designer who builds things. Omar: a vegetable seller at the Eastgate market, Ravi's first customer. Priya: Ravi's sister, who is good with numbers. Eastgate: the market where the story begins. Sunbox: the name of Ravi's invention, a cold box for market stalls that runs on sunlight. All numbers and results in the story are imagined illustrations, not real data, and no currency is named. Farid: a metalworker who works next door to Nadia's workshop and cuts the metal for the Sunbox. Karan: a vegetable seller at Eastgate who once bought a slightly better cloth that nobody noticed. Hana: an apple seller on the apple row at Eastgate. Mina: a flatbread seller with a clever oven of her own design at the far end of the market. Samir: Nadia's uncle, who tried to sell a solar fridge long ago, when it was too early. Ravi mends water pumps at his job. Omar has a moustache. Mrs Dutta: a retired shopkeeper and polite doubter who warns Ravi that sellers are careless and thieves love shiny things. Anita Joshi: a calm investor who has helped small firms and backs Sunbox because she wants a business that lasts. Dev and Salma: the two assemblers the company hires, a quiet young man and a talkative woman. Northfield: the first nearby market the Sunbox reaches after Eastgate. Brightcool: a large company that launches a cheap copy of the Sunbox. Key terms: copying, something new, competition, overlooked problem, small market, timing, small team, price, steady profit, long-lasting advantage, know-how, trust, mission, pitch. Rules of thumb are called rules of thumb and are not laws. Voice: warm, practical, concrete and kind, never preachy. The final beat says this is general information and not financial advice.

beats.summary: Ravi visits Nadia's cluttered workshop, full of tools and half-finished things.

beats.summary: Nadia explains that batteries have also become lighter, cheaper and longer-lasting.

beats.scene: Six stalls with the same new cart and a seventh arriving just behind

beats.summary: Ravi writes a question he will keep asking: why now, and why not before?

beats.summary: Ravi recalls an inventor whose excellent gadget sat unsold on a shelf because nobody explained it.

beats.summary: Priya advises him to talk about the seller's problem, not the machine.

beats.summary: Priya works out the price: it must cover the costs, keep the business alive and let it grow.

beats.summary: Ravi practises thinking for himself: he writes down what he believes, why, and what would prove him wrong.

beats.summary: His list: sellers lose much to heat, a solar box works, and sellers will pay, each with what would prove it wrong.

beats.scene: A calendar with a date circled in red and a small checklist
beats.summary: Ravi sets a date to check each belief against the world instead of hoping.

beats.scene: Nadia reads the notebook list and adds a line with a pencil
beats.summary: Nadia reads the list and adds her own line: do not treat a hunch as a fact.

beats.scene: A retired shopkeeper wags a finger at Ravi beside a locked cabinet
beats.summary: A doubter, Mrs Dutta, tells Ravi why the Sunbox may fail; Ravi listens and adds a lock.

beats.scene: Priya shows a column of costs for a hundred boxes beside a thin purse
beats.summary: The team wants to make a hundred boxes, which costs far more than their savings.

beats.scene: Priya explains investors using two coins and a small tree
beats.summary: Priya explains that investors give money for a share of the company and hope it will grow.

beats.scene: A calm woman in a neat jacket reads a message on her phone
beats.summary: An investor, Anita Joshi, who has helped small firms before, agrees to listen to a short talk.

beats.scene: Priya holds a stopwatch while Ravi talks and papers lie scattered
beats.summary: Ravi's first practice talk is too long and full of details, and Priya times it at almost ten minutes.

beats.scene: A card with three short lines is pinned above Ravi's desk
beats.summary: His pitch has three plain sentences: what Sunbox does, who it helps, and why it can work now.

beats.scene: Nadia leans forward with a frown and plays the part of a hard investor
beats.summary: Nadia plays a tough investor and asks hard questions, such as what happens if a big firm copies them.

beats.scene: Ravi stands before three seated listeners holding a small box
beats.summary: On Friday Ravi stands before three listeners holding a small Sunbox and begins with the problem.

beats.scene: Anita Joshi asks a question and Ravi answers while a colleague takes notes
beats.summary: In the questions that follow, Ravi answers honestly, including saying plainly when he does not know.

beats.scene: Two people shake hands across a table with a document between them
beats.summary: Two offers arrive, and Priya says that choosing a backer is like choosing travel companions who want the same long journey.

beats.scene: Priya reads an agreement with a pencil while a lawyer friend watches
beats.summary: Priya reads the agreement line by line and asks a person who knows the law to check it before they sign.

beats.scene: A bigger workshop with new workers fitting seals at long benches
beats.summary: With money in the bank, the team rents a bigger workshop and hires two assemblers, and Farid joins full time.

beats.scene: A small team laughs together over a meal on the workshop floor
beats.summary: A strong small team grows its own culture, built on people who enjoy the work and trust each other.

beats.scene: Ravi talks with an applicant who holds a toolbox and a smile
beats.summary: Ravi learns to hire people who enjoy the work and trust each other, and not only the most skilled.

beats.scene: Ravi writes a short sentence on a poster above the workshop door
beats.summary: Ravi writes a mission for the company: to help market sellers keep what they grow.

beats.scene: A group of workers carries boxes toward a van at sunrise
beats.summary: A clear mission helps people pull in the same direction and gives meaning to hard work.

beats.scene: Ravi stands by a van with a scratched panel in his hands
beats.summary: A delivered box has a scratched panel, and the mission helps Ravi decide to replace it at once.

beats.scene: Ravi shakes his head at a chart where one line rises very steeply
beats.summary: A big trading company offers to order two thousand boxes in one month, which would make the company grow very fast.

beats.scene: Ravi sits between a steep growth chart and a small calm chart
beats.summary: Ravi sees that growing before the product is proven would spread problems, so he asks for a smaller first order.

beats.scene: A hand holds up a certificate beside a Sunbox on a test bench
beats.summary: Rules matter: food must be kept safe, so the team learns the local rules and has the Sunbox tested.

beats.scene: An inspector checks a Sunbox with a clipboard while Priya waits with papers
beats.summary: The Sunbox passes every test, and rules followed carefully become one more reason for customers to trust the company.

beats.scene: Omar in his best shirt helps unload Sunboxes at Northfield market
beats.summary: Once the first lane is happy, the team brings the Sunbox to Northfield, a nearby market, and Omar tells his story.

beats.scene: A map with five towns joined by a neat line of small flags
beats.summary: They go town by town, only when the last one is working well, and each step looks like the one before.

beats.scene: Dark clouds over a market where a row of Sunboxes sit in grey light
beats.summary: A cloudy week: some boxes cannot make enough power, and the vegetables inside begin to warm.

beats.scene: Nadia and Ravi lean over a failing panel with a cloudy sky behind them
beats.summary: The team adds a larger battery so the cold lasts through dull days, and upgrades every box in the field for free.

beats.scene: A shiny rival product on a stage with a large banner and a crowd
beats.summary: A large rival, Brightcool, with plenty of money, launches a copy of the Sunbox at a much lower price.

beats.scene: Priya reads the rival's price list calmly while Ravi paces the floor
beats.summary: They take the rival's box apart: it copies the shape of the Sunbox but not the lessons learned along the way.

beats.scene: Sellers crowd around Nadia's repair table at the Eastgate market
beats.summary: Customers stay with the Sunbox because it has proved itself, and the team answers every call and fixes problems quickly.

beats.scene: A seller carries a leaking cheap box back to the Sunbox workshop
beats.summary: Some sellers who switched find that the cheaper box leaks, and they return, and the team welcomes them kindly.

beats.scene: Nadia and Ravi sketch an improved model at a crowded workbench
beats.summary: The team does not rest: they improve the Sunbox, staying ahead of copies by learning and building faster.

beats.scene: A single notebook page with the word ahead written and underlined
beats.summary: Priya writes that an advantage is not won once but must be earned again every year.

beats.scene: Farmers load full crates into trucks beside a row of Sunboxes
beats.summary: A new thing that works helps many people at once: sellers lose less, so they order more from farmers.

beats.scene: A shopper opens a bag of fresh greens and smiles at a seller
beats.summary: Shoppers gain too: fresher food on their tables, even at the end of a hot day.

beats.scene: Ravi marks five towns on a map with small flags in a notebook
beats.summary: After three years, in this imagined story, Sunbox is in five towns with about four hundred stalls using it.

beats.scene: Omar shows a newcomer a Sunbox under a wide canopy in another town
beats.summary: Omar, the first customer, now helps new sellers in other towns and has become a friend of the company.

beats.scene: Ravi speaks to a classroom of children at a small school
beats.summary: Ravi is invited to speak at a school, and he tells the children about the bin and the question that kept him awake.

beats.scene: A child in a classroom holds up a drawing of an invention
beats.summary: A girl holds up a drawing of a machine to help her grandmother carry water and asks if she may build it.

beats.scene: Three paths leave one door: to a school, a shop and a village square
beats.summary: The same thinking works beyond business: in a school, a job or a village, anyone can notice what people accept and make something new.

beats.scene: Ravi, Nadia and Priya sit on the workshop roof at sunset with tea
beats.summary: The three friends look back over what they have learned and laugh at how little they knew at the beginning.

beats.scene: Ravi opens a fresh notebook and writes five short lines
beats.summary: Ravi writes the lessons in a fresh notebook: look for what people accept, make something much better, start small, protect it and keep going.

beats.scene: Ravi closes his notebook beside a Sunbox in the morning light
beats.summary: The book ends with a summary: look for what people accept, make something much better, start small, protect it, and keep going; it is general information and not financial advice.

Priya has a job, but she says she will help in the evenings.

Each friend has a reason, but they share one big belief.
Ravi once worked in a team that broke apart in a month.

With separate jobs, friends do not fight over the same task.

B1B2: Ravi is a young engineer who mends water pumps all week. On Saturdays he walks to Eastgate market just after sunrise, when the vegetables are still bright and cool.
By noon the sun climbs above the roofs and strikes the open stalls. Within an hour the spinach hangs limp, and the tomatoes lose their shine.
Ravi's favourite seller, Omar, picks through his tomatoes with quick, tired hands. Every soft one goes into a bin behind the stall, and he does not say a word.
One afternoon Ravi finally asks Omar how often so much food goes into the bin. Omar shrugs and says it happens on every hot day, and that nobody has ever stopped it.
At work, Ravi's job is to find what is broken and make it work again. That habit follows him home, and he cannot see the bin of spoiled food as anything but a problem with an answer.
On his way out of the market, Ravi passes the back lane where the big bins stand. They are full to the top with greens and fruit that were fresh only that morning.
Ravi stops at the gate and asks himself a simple question. Surely somebody has already tried to fix this, so why does the bin still fill up every day?
The next Saturday Ravi arrives with two thermometers and a notebook. He hangs one in the shade of a stall and the other where the sun falls, and writes down both numbers every hour.
When Ravi talks about his worry, his neighbours all give him the same advice. They say the safe thing to do is to open another stall and sell what everyone else sells.
That night Ravi lies awake long after midnight, turning the question over and over. By morning he has decided to find out why such a plain problem has been left alone.
On Sunday Ravi visits his sister Priya, who spends her days keeping accounts for small firms. She listens carefully to his story, and then she puts down her pen.
Priya takes a paper napkin and draws two columns on it. She says there are two kinds of progress, and most people never stop to ask which one they are making.
The first kind, Priya says, is copying what already works. A baker opens a second shop with the same recipes, and now more people can buy good bread.
The second kind is making something that did not exist before. When clean water first came into homes through pipes, daily life in whole towns changed.
The next day, in the pump workshop, Ravi sees the idea in front of him. The office copier makes more of the same, while the half-built machine beside it is something nobody has ever seen.
Priya admits that copying is the safe road for most people who start out. If you do what already works and it fails, nobody blames you, because you followed the crowd.
But copying adds very little to the world, Priya says. Something new is harder to make, yet when it works it can change the lives of thousands at once.
Priya says that copying is like adding one more chair to a room that is already full. Making something new is like opening a door in the wall, so people can walk into a new place.
Priya warns him that the second road is lonely and risky. Most first attempts fail, she says, and nobody can tell him in advance which ones will not.
Ravi tells her he wants to try the second road, even though it frightens him. Priya smiles and says that he must then find a problem worth solving, and not just a clever idea.
On Saturday Ravi brings Priya to the apple row at Eastgate market. Twenty stalls stand side by side, and every one of them sells almost the same red apples.
Near the middle of the row, a seller called Hana lowers her price by a small amount. Some shoppers notice at once and walk over to her stall.
Hana's neighbours see the crowd at her stall and lower their own prices. Soon every seller in the row has done the same, and the shoppers go back to wandering.
By evening nearly every seller has sold all of their apples. Priya adds up the numbers and shows Ravi that they earned less than they did the week before.
Priya explains to Ravi why this always happens in a crowded market. When shoppers cannot tell one seller's apples from another's, the only difference left to compare is the price.
Competition is wonderful for shoppers, who enjoy low prices and plenty of choice. For the sellers, however, it means long days, thin profits and very little left over.
Priya points out a hidden cost of thin profits. A seller with no spare money cannot try new things, so tomorrow looks just like today.
At the far end of the market, they find Mina, who sells hot flatbread from a clever oven nobody else owns. People queue for it, and she sets her own price.
Priya says that a business with no direct rivals does not have to fight over price. It can keep much more of the money it earns, and that gives it room to grow.
That evening Ravi writes a line in his notebook and underlines it. The aim is not to be cheaper than the others, but to be different in a way people truly want.
Back in his small rented room, Ravi writes a question on a whiteboard. What have people simply learned to accept, and could any of it be fixed?
Ravi fills the board with things people accept without complaint. There are long queues, crowded buses, broken street lamps and, near the bottom, the bin behind Omar's stall.
Ravi asks a tea seller what annoys her most about her work. She says nothing does, and then she realises that she stopped noticing her troubles long ago.
At Eastgate, spoiled food is so normal that sellers write it off as a cost of doing business. Because everybody accepts it, nobody has ever tried to measure it or to stop it.
On the next hot Saturday, Ravi stands by the bins with a notebook and a pair of gloves. He counts and weighs everything that the sellers of one lane throw away.
When he adds up the numbers, Ravi can hardly believe them. On a hot day, about one crate in every six goes into the bin, and that is in a single lane.
Ravi shows Omar the numbers, and Omar goes quiet. He says he loses about a day's income every week, but he cannot afford a cold room to stop it.
Big cold rooms do exist, Omar explains, but they stand far outside the town. They cost a great deal to rent, they need mains power, and an open stall has no plug.
Ravi counts the stalls of Eastgate and gets a number in the hundreds. If each one loses even a little every hot day, the total is enormous.
Ravi searches for anybody who has already solved this problem for market sellers. He finds nothing, and he decides that he has found an overlooked problem that is large, real and ignored.
Early one morning, over a crate of onions, Ravi asks Omar a direct question. What would a solution have to be like for him to change the way he works?
Omar thinks for a long moment while he strokes his moustache. If it were only a little better than what he has now, he says, he would not bother, because change costs him time and worry.
Ravi writes much better on his whiteboard and underlines it twice. A new product, he decides, must be so far ahead of what exists that nobody needs convincing.
Ravi remembers a seller called Karan who bought a slightly better cloth to cover his crates. It worked a little better, but nobody noticed, and he gave it up within a month.
Then Ravi thinks of the wheeled carts that arrived at the market years ago. They were so much better than carrying sacks on a shoulder that nobody had to be told to buy one.
Ravi writes down what much better would mean for Omar. The vegetables must stay crisp all day, there must be no cables, and the cost must be smaller than the loss.
Priya turns the card into three clear tests for any invention. It must keep things cold in the sun, work without mains power, and pay for itself within one season.
Ravi tests the two easy ideas first, because they cost the least. Misting fans use too much water and make nothing cold, and blocks of ice melt quickly and must be bought again every single day.
Walking home at noon, Ravi squints at the blazing sun. The same sun that spoils the vegetables is also sending out free power, and nobody is using it for the market.
Ravi checks the idea against Priya's three tests and cannot find a failure. He hurries home with his heart racing, afraid that he will forget it before he can draw.
All night Ravi draws a metal box with a small solar panel on its lid. The box will stay cold by itself, using only the sunlight that falls on the stall.
He works out, one step at a time, how the box should work. The panel turns sunlight into electricity, a small cooling unit chills the inside, and thick walls stop the cold from escaping.
Ravi gets stuck on the cooling part of the plan. He understands the idea, but he has never built a real box, and a drawing cannot do that for him.
Then Ravi thinks of Nadia, an old friend who is a designer and who builds things for a living. He calls her at once, even though it is nearly midnight.
Nadia's workshop is a cheerful mess of tools, wood shavings and half-finished chairs. She clears a corner of her workbench with one sweep of her arm and tells Ravi to show her the drawing.
Nadia taps the drawing with her pencil and asks who the box is for. Ravi tells her about Omar and the bin, and shows her the numbers from his notebook.
Then Nadia starts to poke holes in the idea, as a good friend should. The box must be light enough to carry, safe in the rain, hard to steal and steady on a wobbly table.
Nadia agrees to help, but she adds one condition to her promise. They must build something real within a month, because a drawing, she says, never taught anybody anything.
They need a name, and they argue about it for an hour. In the end they call the invention Sunbox, because it is simple, and Nadia paints it on a crate in bright letters.
On the first Saturday of their month, they go shopping for parts. They buy a small solar panel, a cooling plate, a fan and sheets of thick foam for the walls.
Ravi spreads a big map on the workshop floor and dreams aloud about every seller in the country. Nadia listens, and then she says that everywhere is a very good way to end up nowhere.
Priya draws a small circle inside a big one on a sheet of paper. She says that the best way to win a large market is to win a small one completely first.
Priya explains that a small market has real advantages for a beginner. It is easy to reach, easy to learn from and easy to serve well, and good news travels fast between neighbours.
Ravi takes a map of Eastgate market and a yellow pencil. He colours in one small corner, the lane of vegetable sellers, and decides that this is where they will begin.
Ravi stands at the market gate with a list of thirty stall names. He has chosen that number carefully, because it is small enough that he can meet every seller in a single week.
Over the next week Ravi visits stall after stall in the lane. Every seller tells him the same story about the heat, and they all talk to one another every day.
Ravi writes down what makes a good small market. The people in it must have the same need, they must be close together, and no strong rival should already serve them.
Nadia tells a story about a friend who tried to open shops in ten towns at once. He could not look after any of them properly, and within a year all ten had closed.
Ravi draws arrows on his wall map from the first lane to the nearby markets. Once the first group is happy, he says, growing to the next one is a natural step.
Priya smiles because she likes the picture of the ripples so much. Growth, she says, should move outward one ring at a time, and everything depends on the small centre being strong.
Nadia arrives with a thick catalogue of solar panels and puts it on the bench. Ravi turns the pages and is surprised at how small the prices have become.

Priya writes a note in the margin of the notebook. An advantage, she says, is not won once and kept forever, because know-how, size and trust must all be earned again every year.

In short, look for what people have stopped noticing, make something much better, start small, and protect it. This book is general information and is not financial advice.

At that hour, just after sunrise, the whole place looked like a painting, with tomatoes glowing in neat pyramids and bundles of spinach still wet with morning dew. He loved the noise, the smell of coriander and the friendly shouting of the sellers as they set up for the day.

Around noon the sun cleared the roofs and fell directly on the open stalls, and the cheerful painting began to fade. Spinach sagged over the edges of its crates, lettuces turned the colour of old paper, and the tomatoes lost their gloss as quickly as a bubble loses its shine. The sellers splashed water on their goods and draped wet cloths over them, but the heat was patient and the cloths dried within minutes.

Omar, the seller Ravi had bought from for years, picked through his tomatoes with quick and tired hands. Each soft one went into a battered bin behind the stall, where it joined the wilted herbs and the cracked cucumbers of the morning. He did it without a word or a sigh, the way a person brushes crumbs from a table.

Ravi finally asked Omar how frequently such a quantity of perfectly good food ended up in that bin. Omar shrugged as though the question were about the weather, and said that it happened on every hot day and always had. Nobody at Eastgate, he added, had ever thought of it as anything but part of the job.

All week long Ravi's job was to find what had broken and persuade it to work again, and the habit did not stay at the office. When he looked at the bin behind Omar's stall, he did not see bad luck or the weather; he saw a fault, and faults, in his experience, had causes. Causes, in turn, sometimes had answers, which is a dangerous thought for a person who already likes tinkering.

On his way out Ravi took the back lane, where the big bins stood in a row beside the wall. They were heaped with greens, onions and fruit that had been perfectly fresh at sunrise, and a few thin dogs and a flock of crows were already taking an interest. It struck him that every item in those bins had once been grown, carried, weighed and carefully arranged, and then simply thrown away.

Standing at the market gate with his bag of slightly bruised plums, Ravi asked himself the simplest of questions. Surely someone cleverer, richer or better connected than he was had already tried to solve this, and surely they had succeeded. Yet the evidence behind him, in the shape of a bin that filled again every single day, suggested otherwise.

The following Saturday Ravi arrived with two thermometers, a notebook and the stubborn look of a man on a mission. He hung one in the shade of a stall and the other in the full glare of the sun, and every hour he wrote down both readings like a patient scientist. By the afternoon the difference was so large that even the sellers, who had been watching him with amusement, stopped laughing and leaned in to look.

When Ravi spoke about his worry, his neighbours offered kind and sensible advice: open another stall, sell what everybody sells, and wait for the customers to arrive. It was the path that thousands of people had walked before him, which was exactly its attraction. Nobody could blame him for failing at something so familiar, and perhaps nobody would even notice if he did.

That night Ravi lay awake long after midnight, turning the question over like a coin he could not bring himself to spend. The sensible choice was to forget it and open a stall, as everybody advised, but sensible choices had never kept him awake. By dawn he had decided to find out, as carefully as he could, why such a plain problem had been left alone for so long.

On Sunday Ravi visited his sister Priya, who spent her days untangling the accounts of small firms and her evenings pretending not to. She listened to the whole story of the thermometers, the bin and the sleepless night without interrupting once, which was unusual for her. Then she put down her pen, folded her hands and gave him the look she reserved for serious ideas.

Priya pulled a paper napkin towards her and divided it into two columns with a single firm line. She explained that progress comes in two quite different kinds, and that most people never pause to ask which of the two they are making. The distinction, she promised, would save him years of confusion and a good deal of expensive effort.

The first kind, Priya said, is copying what already works, and she gave the example of a baker who opens a second shop with exactly the same recipes. More families can now buy good bread without crossing the town, and nobody should sneer at that. It is real progress, but it is progress of a particular kind, because the world gains more of something it already had.

The second kind, Priya continued, is making something that did not exist before, and she asked him to imagine the first town that received clean water through pipes. Women and children no longer spent their mornings hauling heavy buckets, and the sickness that follows contaminated water began to fade. Nobody had copied anything, she said; somebody had simply imagined a thing that was not there and then built it.

On Monday, in the pump workshop, Ravi found the idea standing right in front of him. The photocopier by the door made more of whatever it was given, faithfully and without end, while the half-finished machine on the bench next to it was something nobody had ever seen. One was an echo and the other was a question, and he realised he had always been more interested in questions.

Priya was honest about the attractions of the first road, which is that it is safe, familiar and easy to explain at family dinners. If a person copies what already works and still fails, the blame is shared with everybody who did the same, and sympathy flows in. The second road offers no such comfort, since a person who tries something new and fails has nobody to blame but himself.

The difficulty, Priya went on, is that copying adds very little to what the world already has, however diligently it is done. Something new is harder and slower to make, and most attempts end in failure, but when one succeeds it can change the lives of thousands of people at once. Ravi noticed that she said the last part quietly, as though she were afraid of how much she meant it.

Priya offered him a picture to keep: copying is like adding one more chair to a room that is already crowded with chairs. Making something new is like finding a closed door in the far wall, opening it, and discovering a whole new space beyond. People would come to the room for the chair, she said, but they would remember the door.

She did not hide the cost, however, and she warned him that the second road is lonely and risky in equal measure. Most first attempts fail, nobody can say in advance which ones will survive, and the people who encourage you at the start are rarely around at the bad moments. Ravi listened closely, because he trusted her more than any adviser he had ever met.

Ravi told her that he wanted to try the second road, even though the thought of it made his stomach tighten. Priya smiled, tore the napkin along its fold and gave him the half that said something new. A clever idea was not enough, she said, because he needed a problem worth solving, and she suspected he had already found one in a bin at Eastgate market.

On Saturday Ravi brought Priya to the apple row at Eastgate, a long lane where twenty stalls stood shoulder to shoulder. Every one of them sold almost exactly the same red apples, piled in the same neat pyramids and guarded by sellers with the same hopeful smile. Priya took out her notebook, as she always did when she smelled a lesson.

Near the middle of the row a seller named Hana quietly rubbed out her price and wrote a slightly lower one in its place. Within a minute some of the shoppers who had been drifting past turned around and walked over to her stall, and her face lit with the pleasure of a small victory. Priya glanced at her watch and murmured that the pleasure would last about ten minutes.

Hana's neighbours saw the little crowd at her stall and understood immediately what had happened, and one by one they rubbed out their own prices. Within the hour every card along the row carried the same low number, and Hana's advantage had evaporated like a puddle in the sun. The shoppers, who now found no reason to prefer her, went back to wandering from stall to stall.

By evening nearly every seller on the row had sold out, and they went home tired but contented, believing they had had a good day. Priya sat on an upturned crate and added up the numbers, and the answer, which she showed to Ravi without comment, was that each of them had earned less than the week before. They had worked harder for a smaller reward, and none of them realised it.

Priya explained, with the patience of a teacher, why it always goes exactly this way. When shoppers cannot tell one seller's apples from another's, the only difference left to compare is the price, and the cheapest seller wins until somebody becomes cheaper still. The race has no natural finishing line, so it ends only when the sellers have nothing left to cut.

Competition, Ravi realised, is wonderful for shoppers, who enjoy low prices, plenty of choice and the pleasure of a bargain. For the sellers it is a treadmill, with long days, thin profits and almost nothing left over at the end of the week. He could not decide whether to admire the system or to feel sorry for the people inside it.

Priya pointed out a hidden cost of thin profits that most people never think about. A seller with no money to spare cannot buy better equipment, test a new idea or survive one bad week, so tomorrow is doomed to look exactly like today. Crowded markets, she said, are not only unrewarding; they are also strangely stuck, like a cart in deep mud.

At the far end of the market, away from the crowd, they found Mina, who sold hot flatbread from a clever oven of her own design that nobody else in Eastgate possessed. A patient queue stretched from her stall, and when somebody asked about the price she simply named it, without glancing at anyone else's. She was not fighting a battle at all, because there was nobody on her side of the field.

Priya summed up the lesson while they stood in the warm smell of bread and watched the queue shuffle forward. A business with no direct rivals does not have to fight over price, so it keeps a fair share of the value it creates and has money left to improve and to grow. She added a warning, though, that standing alone is only useful if enough people truly want what you offer.

That evening Ravi wrote a single line in his notebook and underlined it twice. The aim, he decided, was not to be a little cheaper or a little cleverer than the people around him, but to be different in a way that customers would truly want. It sounded simple enough on paper, which was precisely why he took it as a warning rather than a comfort.

Back in his small rented room, Ravi propped a whiteboard against the wall and wrote a question across the top in large, careful letters. What have people simply learned to accept, he asked, and could any of it be different? Priya had told him that the best problems hide inside things that nobody notices any more, because familiarity makes even a bad thing look like a law of nature.

Ravi filled the whiteboard with things people accepted without complaint: long queues at the bank, crowded buses, street lamps that stayed broken for months. Looking at the list as a whole, he felt as though he had been wearing a pair of glasses that made everything ordinary and had only now taken them off.
