At Eastgate, spoiled food had become so normal that the sellers treated it as a fixed cost of doing business, like rent or the price of string. Because everybody accepted the loss, nobody had bothered to measure it, and because nobody had measured it, nobody could say how large it truly was. It was a problem hidden in plain sight, protected only by its own familiarity and by everyone's habit of looking away.

On the next hot Saturday Ravi stationed himself beside the bins with a notebook, a pair of old gloves and a bathroom scale borrowed from his landlady. All day long he counted and weighed whatever the sellers of a single lane threw away, ignoring the curious looks and one rather rude comment. It was dull, smelly work, but he knew that a number would persuade people when a feeling never could.

When he added up the numbers that evening, Ravi could hardly believe the total. On a hot day, in this lane alone, about one crate in every six had gone into the bin, and the lane was only one of dozens in the market. If the figures held for the rest of Eastgate, the waste was not a nuisance but a river of good food flowing quietly out of the gate.

Ravi showed Omar the numbers he had gathered, and for a long moment the usually talkative stallholder said nothing at all. He admitted that he lost food worth about a full day's income every week, and then he shrugged helplessly, since a cold room was a luxury he could not possibly afford. The weariness in his voice told Ravi far more than the figures had managed to tell him.

Big cold rooms did exist, Omar explained, but they stood on the far edge of town beside the main road, and renting a corner of one cost more than he could afford. They also needed steady mains power, and an open stall in a market, with a canvas roof and a tangle of borrowed wires, had nothing of the kind. For sellers like him, the usual solution was simply out of reach, and had been for as long as anyone could remember.

Ravi walked the whole market with a clicker in his pocket, counting stalls, and the total came to several hundred. If each of them lost even a modest share of its stock on every hot day, the waste across Eastgate over a single summer was far greater than he had dared to imagine. And Eastgate, he reminded himself, was only one market among the many that fed the surrounding towns.

Before he allowed himself to feel excited, Ravi spent a week searching for anyone who had already solved the problem for market sellers, and he found nobody. There were big cold stores for big companies, and nothing at all for a man with a canvas roof and a crate of tomatoes. He wrote the words overlooked problem at the top of a clean page, and for the first time since the sleepless night he felt that he knew where he was standing.

Early one morning, as the two men sat on crates over a pot of sweet tea, Ravi put a direct question to Omar. What would a solution have to be like, he asked, before a busy seller would bother to change the way he worked? He had learned that the answer to that question was worth more than any number of clever designs.

Omar thought for a long moment, stroking his moustache and watching a pigeon steal a grain of rice from the ground. If the answer were only a little better than what he did now, he said, he would not bother, because every change costs a seller time, money and worry, and he had very little of any of them. The new thing would have to make the old way look foolish, and not merely a little out of date.

Ravi wrote the words much better on his whiteboard and underlined them twice, so heavily that the pen squeaked. A new product, he decided, must be so far ahead of the old way that nobody needs to be persuaded, because the advantage is obvious to anyone who sees it for a minute. Slightly better, by contrast, is the mark of ideas that feel clever to their makers and unnecessary to everyone else.

Ravi remembered a seller named Karan who had once paid for a slightly better cloth to cover his crates. It kept the sun off a little more effectively than the old one, but the improvement was too small for anyone to see, and within a month Karan had gone back to the old cloth to save the money. A change that nobody can feel is a change that nobody will pay for.

Then Ravi thought of the wheeled carts that had arrived at the market some years earlier. They were so much better than carrying sacks on a shoulder that no salesman was needed, since sellers saw one roll past with a load that would have bent a strong man double and asked where they could buy it. That, he decided, was the standard he had to meet, and nothing less would do.

On a card at a corner table, Ravi wrote down what much better would mean for a man like Omar. The vegetables would have to stay crisp from dawn until the last customer left, the answer must need no cables or plugs, and its price must be smaller than the food it saved. Each demand was reasonable when taken by itself, but together they formed a mountain that would take real work to climb.

Priya, who liked her requirements countable, turned the card into three plain tests that any invention would have to pass. It must keep food cold in the open sun, it must work without any connection to mains power, and it must pay for itself within a single selling season. If an idea failed even one of the tests, she said, it was a hobby and not a business.

Ravi tried the easy ideas first, because easy ideas are the cheapest of all to disprove. Misting fans used a great deal of water and made nothing truly cold, while blocks of ice melted by noon and had to be bought afresh every day, which turned a small saving into a large permanent expense. Neither idea passed all three of Priya's tests, and he crossed both out with some relief, as one closes a door that leads nowhere.

Walking home at noon with his hat in his hand, Ravi squinted at the blazing sun and felt an idea begin to form. The same sun that spoiled the vegetables was also pouring out free energy, and a panel on a roof could turn that energy into electricity that needed no cable at all. The enemy, it suddenly occurred to him, might be persuaded to become the servant, if only he could work out how.

By the time he reached his door Ravi had checked the idea against Priya's three tests in his head, and on paper, at least, he could not find a single failure. He hurried upstairs with his heart racing, convinced that he would lose the thread if he stopped for so much as a glass of water. Sometimes the best ideas, he had noticed over the years, arrive looking exactly like a risk, and that was how this one felt.

All night, by the light of a single lamp, Ravi drew a metal box with a small solar panel fixed to its lid. In his sketch the sunlight fell on the panel, the panel fed a little cooling unit, and the inside of the box stayed cold long after the cloth over a stall would have dried out. It was a crude drawing, but it was the first time the whole idea had been visible on one page.

Ravi worked out, step by step and with growing excitement, how such a box should behave. The panel would turn sunlight into electricity, a small cooling unit would use that electricity to chill the air inside, and thick walls packed with insulation would slow the heat that kept trying to creep back in. Each part was ordinary and already known; the novelty lay in putting them together for a man with a canvas roof.

Eventually Ravi got stuck on the cooling part, where the calculations began to wobble like a table with one short leg. He understood the principle perfectly well, but he had spent his career with pumps and pipes, and he had never turned a drawing into a real object with real hinges. Somebody had to hold the tools, and it was clear that the somebody could not be him.

Then he thought of Nadia, an old friend from university who was a designer and who built things for a living, from chairs to bicycle trailers. He telephoned her immediately, even though it was nearly midnight, and she answered on the second ring with the cheerful suspicion of a person who knows that late calls mean trouble. Come to the workshop tomorrow, she told him, and bring the drawing with you.

Nadia's workshop was a cheerful disaster of tools, wood shavings, paint tins and half-finished chairs, lit by a window the size of a barn door. She cleared a corner of the workbench with one sweep of her arm and told Ravi to spread out his drawing. For a minute she said nothing at all, which he knew from long experience was a good sign, because she only talked when she was unimpressed.

Nadia tapped the drawing with the end of her pencil and asked the only question that mattered: who was it for, and had he asked them? Ravi told her everything about Omar, the bin, the thermometers and the lane where one crate in six was lost. She listened to the whole story with her arms folded, and when he had finished she nodded slowly.

Then Nadia began to poke holes in the idea, which is what good friends do, and she did it with remarkable thoroughness. The box would have to be light enough to carry, strong enough to survive the rain, awkward enough to discourage thieves and stable enough to sit on a table with one short leg. Ravi wrote every objection in his notebook, and by the end the list had grown longer than the drawing.

To his enormous relief, Nadia agreed to help, though she attached a single condition to her promise. Within one month they must have something real standing on the bench, because a drawing, she said, had never taught anybody anything that a prototype could not teach faster. Ravi shook her hand so enthusiastically that she laughed out loud and had to rescue her fingers from him.

They needed a name, and they argued about it for an hour over cold tea and half a packet of biscuits. Ravi favoured something technical with initials, Nadia wanted something that a seller could say with a full mouth, and in the end they agreed to call the invention Sunbox. She painted the word across an old crate in bright yellow letters, and it looked like the beginning of something.

On the first Saturday of their month they went shopping for parts, and they came back with a small solar panel, a cooling plate, a quiet fan and several large sheets of thick foam for the walls. The shopkeeper, who had assumed they were building a refrigerator for a school project, was visibly confused when Nadia explained the real plan. Ravi did not mind; confusion, he had decided, was the normal first reaction to anything new.

Ravi spread a huge map across the workshop floor and began to dream aloud about every seller in every market in the country. Nadia listened with a paintbrush behind her ear, and when he finally ran out of breath she remarked that trying to serve everyone at once is an excellent way of serving nobody. Big dreams were welcome in the workshop, she said, but a first customer is a person, not a map.

Priya drew a small circle inside a big one on a sheet of graph paper and tapped the little one with her pen. The way to win a large market, she told them, is usually to win a small one so completely that nobody there would dream of using anything else. Only after that could they start thinking about the big circle, and not a day sooner.

A small market, Priya explained, has real advantages for a beginner: it is easy to reach, easy to learn from and easy to serve extremely well. Everybody in it knows everybody else, so a satisfied customer becomes an advertisement and an unhappy one becomes a warning. In a large market, by contrast, a young company can shout all day and never be heard.

Ravi took a map of Eastgate market and a yellow pencil and studied it for a long while. Then he coloured in one small corner, the crowded lane where the vegetable sellers worked shoulder to shoulder, and announced that this was the place where the Sunbox would either live or die. It was a surprisingly small patch of paper for such a large and frightening decision.

Ravi stood at the market gate holding a list of thirty stalls in the vegetable lane, written out in his neatest handwriting. He had chosen the number with care, because it was small enough for him to meet every seller in a single week, and large enough that success would mean something real. Thirty customers, he thought, were a very different thing from thirty thousand, and a far more manageable place to begin.

Over the following week Ravi visited stall after stall in the lane, and everywhere he heard the same story, told in different words and with different sighs. The heat was cruel, the losses were routine and nobody believed anything could be done. He also noticed that the sellers chatted to one another all day, which meant that whatever one of them thought of the Sunbox, the rest would hear about by lunch.

That evening Ravi wrote down what made a good small market, so that he would recognise the next one when it came. The people in it must share an urgent need, they must live or work in close proximity, and no strong rival should already be serving them well. If any one of those three conditions was missing, he suspected, the market would prove much harder to win than it looked.

To prove the point, Nadia told them about a friend who had opened shops in ten towns at the same moment, full of confidence and borrowed money. He could not give any single shop the attention it needed, the customers in each town were disappointed, and within a year every one of them had closed. Spread thin, she said, a company is like a little butter across far too much bread, and nobody tastes it.

On the wall map Ravi drew arrows leading outward from the first lane to the nearby markets, and from there to the rest of the town. Once the first group of sellers was truly happy, he explained, moving to the next would be a natural step and not a leap of faith, because each new group would look much like the one before. The plan resembled a stone dropped in a pond, with rings that grow one after another.

Priya loved the picture of the ripples spreading across the pond and said so with unusual warmth. Growth, she told them, should travel outward one ring at a time, and every ring depends on the strength of the small centre from which it began. A company that rushes outward before its centre is solid, she added, makes waves for about a minute and then vanishes.

Nadia arrived at the workshop with a thick catalogue of solar panels and dropped it on the bench with a thud. Ravi turned the pages, comparing the figures with what he remembered from his student days, and was startled at how small the prices had become. What had once been an expensive curiosity for specialists was now something an ordinary person could buy on a modest budget.

Ravi remembered a teacher from his student days who had once laughed kindly at the idea of a solar cooling box. In those days, the teacher had said, panels were too heavy, too weak and far too expensive to run anything useful, and he had been perfectly right. The teacher had not been wrong about the world; the world had simply changed since.

Nadia set a small modern battery on the bench beside a huge old one that looked like a brick and weighed about as much as a small child. Batteries, she explained, had become lighter, cheaper and far more durable over the years, and without that quiet change a box that kept its cold through a cloudy afternoon would still be a fantasy. Ravi marvelled that so important a thing had happened without anybody making a speech.

Priya listened to the two of them and then summed it up in a sentence. Timing matters enormously, she said, because an idea that was impossible a decade ago can be perfectly possible today, and the people who notice the change first have a head start. The world was quietly holding a door open, and Ravi had happened to be standing nearby.

Nadia drew a clock face on the workshop wall with two labels, too early on the left and too late on the right. A company that arrives too early finds that the world is not ready for what it offers, while one that arrives too late discovers that somebody else has already made the same thing and done it better. The art, she said, was to hit the small gap between the two, and that gap changes every year.

Nadia told them about her uncle Samir, who had tried to sell a solar fridge to market sellers many years earlier. His idea was sound and his machine worked, but it cost so much that nobody could afford one, and he abandoned the whole project after two seasons. He was not a fool, she said; he was simply early, and being early looks exactly like being wrong.

Then she gave an example of what arriving too late looks like in practice. A seller who buys the same cart that six of his neighbours already use has nothing special to offer, so the crowd closes around him like water around a dropped stone, and the market hardly notices that he exists. Good timing, she said, is not luck; it is the habit of asking what has changed.

On his whiteboard Ravi wrote a question and drew a box around it so that he would never forget to ask it again. Why is now the right time for this idea, he demanded, and what has changed that made it impossible before and possible today? An honest answer, he knew, would be worth more than any amount of enthusiasm.

Ravi visited a supplier on the edge of town and asked whether the prices were likely to keep falling. The man, who looked as if he had been selling panels since the dawn of time, pulled out lists from earlier years and laid them side by side, and the numbers sloped downwards like a gentle hillside. Nobody could promise the future, he said, but the direction had been the same for a very long time.

Ravi checked one last thing, which was whether the sellers themselves were ready to try something new. Eastgate was busier every year, most of the sellers now carried phones that they used to order stock and to take payments, and the heat seemed to bite harder with every season. For the first time he felt, with a tingle of excitement, that the timing was right.

Late one night Ravi and Nadia sat staring at a list of tasks that had grown to fill three pages. There was far too much work for two people, and neither of them could be trusted to keep honest accounts or even to remember what the last month's parts had cost. They both knew who could, but neither wanted to be the first to say her name.

Priya hesitated at first, because she had a steady job, a careful nature and a healthy respect for the way new businesses die. After a week of thinking and several long phone calls with her brother, she agreed to help in the evenings and to keep the accounts, though she insisted on keeping her job for now. It was the most generous kind of yes, because it came with her eyes open.

On the first evening the three of them sat around a small table under a single lamp, drinking tea from mismatched cups. It felt less like a company than a long conversation among friends, and nobody wished to spoil it with grand titles or complicated charts. Yet something was settling between them, quietly and without any announcement, the way sediment settles in clear water.

Each of the three had a different private reason for joining the little company, and they were happy to admit it. Ravi wanted to solve the problem that had kept him awake, Nadia wanted to build something that mattered, and Priya wanted to prove that careful, sensible work could change a market. What bound them together was not friendship alone but a shared belief that the Sunbox was worth the trouble, and that belief was worth more than any contract.

Ravi remembered a project group from his university days that had fallen apart within a month, loudly and with a great deal of wounded pride. Its members had wanted quite different things from the work, and they discovered the difference only when the work became difficult and somebody had to give way. Beliefs that are not shared, he reflected, tend to stay hidden until the day they cost the most.

They agreed that each of them would have one clear job, and they wrote the three jobs on separate cards so that nobody could forget. Nadia would build the boxes, Ravi would find the customers and persuade them, and Priya would look after every number that touched money. If anything fell into the gaps between the cards, they would talk about it openly rather than quietly assume it was somebody else's problem.

Clear jobs, Priya pointed out, have a hidden benefit that most new teams never think about. When each person owns a different task, nobody competes with a friend for the same job, nobody is confused about who is responsible for a result, and credit is easy to share because it is easy to see. Many a friendship, she added, has been quietly ruined by two people who both thought they were in charge.

They pinned the three cards in a row above the workbench and decided to meet every Monday morning for a brief talk. Each person said what had been done the previous week, what was planned for the next one and what help was needed, and the meeting was forbidden from lasting longer than a cup of tea. The routine was dull on purpose, because dull routines are what keep exciting plans alive.

Soon the little team had its first honest disagreement, which arrived over something as small as a hinge. Nadia wanted the first box to be perfect, with a hidden hinge and a polished lid, while Ravi wanted to put something rough in front of Omar that very week, and the argument grew warm before it grew sensible. They settled on three weeks, which was too long for him and too short for her, and Priya observed that this was how she knew it was fair.

Priya insisted that they put the ownership of the company in writing, however awkward the conversation might be. Friends who agree in advance who owns what, she argued, are far more likely to remain friends when the company succeeds or when it fails, because neither outcome is a surprise. They signed the paper with three different pens and then, relieved, went to find something to eat.

Next door to Nadia's workshop worked Farid, a metalworker with forearms like tree roots, who had been watching the strange project through the open door with growing curiosity. One afternoon he walked in, studied the drawing for a full minute and offered to cut the sheets for the first frame at a fair price. By evening the first shining panels of the Sunbox lay on the bench, and the sparks from his cutter were still fading in the air.

Nadia lined the walls with thick layers of foam and sealed every joint with tape, working with the concentration of a surgeon. Heat, she told Ravi, behaves like water, since it will find the smallest crack and creep in until the whole inside is warm again. A good box was therefore less about making cold than about refusing to let it escape.

After two weeks of long evenings the first Sunbox stood on the bench, dented here and there but unmistakably a box. Ravi taped a thermometer inside the lid, because he knew that a product has to be truly excellent in its own right before any amount of clever selling can rescue it. Charm and marketing might fool a customer once, but a box that failed to keep tomatoes cold would never fool the tomatoes.

They carried the box into the sunny yard behind the workshop, switched it on and sat down to wait with the nervous patience of expectant parents. After two hours the thermometer showed that the inside was barely colder than the air outside, and Nadia, who had put so much of herself into the box, said nothing at all. Ravi felt the particular disappointment of a beautiful plan meeting the stubborn facts of the real world.

Ravi carried the box into a dark room, shone a torch around the edge of the lid and saw thin lines of light leaking through gaps that nobody had noticed. If light could get in, he reasoned, then so could warm air, and every gap was quietly undoing the work of the whole machine. They fitted a thick rubber seal along the edge, doubled the foam in the lid and tested again the next morning.

The second test gave a much better result, and the thermometer inside fell by several degrees within the first hour. But as the sun climbed, the edge of the lid threw a thin shadow across one corner of the panel, and the cooling slowed as if the box had grown tired. Nadia moved the panel, tilted it towards the sun and fixed it on a small frame that the shadow could not reach.

In the third test the box stayed pleasantly cold until a large cloud drifted across the sun, and then, without light, the panel's power dwindled and the inside began to warm within minutes. The failure was a useful one, because it showed that the box needed some way of holding on to the power it made during the bright hours. A market stall, after all, cannot ask the weather to be polite, and a box that depends on perfect skies is only a toy.

Nadia fitted a small battery into the space beside the cooling unit, wired it in with the care of a person defusing something, and stood back. The battery stored the power that the panel made during the bright hours and released it whenever the sun disappeared, so the box no longer cared whether the sky was clear. When the next cloud arrived, the thermometer held steady, and the three of them cheered as though a goal had been scored.

To make the test fair, Priya insisted on a control: the same kind of tomatoes, bought in the same shop at the same hour, would sit in the Sunbox and in an ordinary crate placed beside it. Both would stay in the same sun for an entire day, and she would note down the condition of each every hour on a chart. If the result favoured the box, she wanted it to be a result that nobody could argue with.

By evening the difference was plain enough for a child to read from across the yard. The tomatoes inside the Sunbox were firm, glossy and cool to the touch, while those in the ordinary crate had wrinkled and slumped like tired travellers after a long journey. Nadia wiped her hands on her apron and said that the box was finally good enough to show to Omar, and nobody felt like arguing.

Nadia patted the finished box as if it were a sleeping animal and declared that something this good would sell itself. Ravi, who remembered several sad stories from his university days, was not so sure, because even the very best products seldom manage to do that. Good work, he suspected, still needs someone to carry it across the last gap, from the bench to the customer's hands.

Ravi remembered an inventor who had lived in his old neighbourhood, a gentle man with ink on his fingers and a drawer full of marvellous gadgets. One of them, a self-winding lamp, was truly clever, but it sat on a dusty shelf in a corner shop for years, because the inventor was too shy to explain it to anyone. The lamp had not failed; it had simply never been introduced to the people who would have loved it.

Selling, Ravi decided, was nothing more mysterious than explaining one idea to one person at a time, and he told himself so repeatedly. It sounded easy on paper, but he was shy by nature, and when he rehearsed in front of the mirror his voice shook like a leaf in the wind. He had spent years persuading pumps to work, and persuading people felt like another language.

On Monday morning Ravi shook hands with Karan, the seller who had once bought a slightly better cloth, and began his first real sales talk. He spoke eagerly about solar panels, cooling plates and battery capacity, and he did not pause for breath for several minutes, convinced that the facts would speak for themselves. Karan nodded politely, glanced at his queue of customers and said that he would think about it, which Ravi would soon learn was how people say no.

Looking back on the whole disappointing morning, Ravi could see exactly where the talk had gone wrong. Karan's eyes had glazed over at about the second mention of the cooling plate, because the whole speech had been about the machine and nothing at all about Karan's troubles. People do not buy parts and clever designs, Ravi realised, but relief from something that hurts.

Priya listened to the whole sad story with a straight face and then gave him a single piece of advice. Begin with the seller's problem, she said, in the seller's own words, and mention the machine only when the seller is already nodding and wondering whether there is an answer. A good salesman, she added, is mostly a good listener who happens to carry a solution.

Ravi practised on Nadia in the workshop until she begged for mercy and threatened him with a hammer. His new opening was a single question, which he repeated in a dozen different voices: how many tomatoes do you throw away on a hot day? It was a humble sentence, but it put the seller at the centre of the story and Ravi in the humble role of someone who had come to help.

On his second attempt Ravi walked up to a woman who sold tomatoes at the end of the lane and asked her, quite simply, how many she threw away on a hot day. She laughed, then sighed, then began to tell him about her week, and by the time he opened the lid of the Sunbox she was leaning over it with her eyes wide. He had not made a speech at all; he had asked a question and then waited.

Ravi learned that one visit is rarely enough, and so he began to visit each seller three times within a fortnight, always at a quiet hour. He kept a list of every question he was asked and every worry that was mentioned, and he promised nothing that the box could not do. Slowly the notebook became a detailed map of what the sellers really thought, feared and hoped for.

Ravi noticed that sellers trusted the people they saw every week, and distrusted the clever strangers who arrived with a speech and then vanished. He decided to be at the market every Saturday at dawn, carrying a flask of tea and no sales pitch at all, simply to listen and to help carry crates. Trust, he understood, is built in small portions, like a wall built brick by brick.

On a hot Saturday Ravi pulled a handcart to Omar's stall at dawn, with the Sunbox wrapped in a blanket like a sleeping child. He asked Omar to try it for just one day, for nothing, with no promises on either side. Omar, who had been disappointed by salesmen before, looked at it for a long moment and then said that he supposed it could not do any harm.

By midday the sun was fierce, and the neighbouring sellers had drifted over, one by one, to watch what was happening at Omar's stall. Some of them were curious, a few were doubtful and one or two were quietly hoping that the strange shining box would fail, since a neighbour's success is not always welcome news. Ravi sat on a crate and tried to look more confident than he felt.

Omar kept half of his lettuces in the Sunbox and half on the table, as Ravi had suggested, so that anyone could compare them. By two o'clock the ones on the table had gone limp and dull, while those inside the box were as crisp as they had been at sunrise, and a small crowd of shoppers had begun to gather. Even the doubtful neighbours leaned in to touch the leaves, and one of them whistled softly under his breath.

Passing shoppers began to notice, with the sharp eyes of people who live for a bargain, that something unusual was happening at the stall. They asked Omar why his lettuces looked so fresh on such a hot afternoon, and he proudly pointed at the shining box, as if he had invented it himself. Ravi, listening from his crate, felt a warmth that had nothing to do with the sun.

By evening Omar had sold nearly everything he had brought, and the bin behind his stall was almost empty, which had not happened on a hot day for as long as he could remember. He sat down on his stool, counted his coins twice, and then counted them a third time, as though the number might change if he looked away. It did not, and a slow and slightly disbelieving smile spread across his tired face.

Omar looked up from his coins and told Ravi, with great seriousness, that he wished to keep the box and was willing to pay for it. He counted the money slowly into Ravi's open hand, as if each coin were a promise, and in that quiet moment the Sunbox ceased to be an experiment and became a business. Ravi found that he could not speak for a moment, and so he simply nodded and closed his fingers over the coins.

That night Ravi laid the coins on Priya's table, and she studied them with the gravity of a jeweller. A first payment is tiny in size, she told him, but enormous in meaning, because it proves that a real person valued the box more than the money he handed over. Compliments, by contrast, cost nothing to give and therefore prove almost nothing about what people really value.

Priya sat down with a pencil and a calculator to work out a proper price for the box. She added up the parts, the labour, the future repairs and a small amount for the unexpected, because a company must earn more than it spends if it intends to survive and grow. When she wrote the figure on a card, it was higher than Ravi had hoped and lower than Nadia had feared.

Priya explained the danger of setting the price too low, which was the mistake Ravi had been tempted to make out of gratitude. Customers might decide that the product was unimportant, and the company would never earn enough to repair, improve and stand behind it. The right price, she said, was a fair share of what the box saved the seller, so that both sides could feel they had made a good bargain.

Omar told everybody about the box, in the loud and delighted voice of a man who has found a treasure, and by Monday three of his neighbours had asked Ravi for a demonstration. It was exactly what Priya had predicted about a small market, where good news travels faster than any advertisement and carries far more weight. Ravi wrote their names on the list of thirty with a hand that was almost trembling.

Priya placed a small plant in a pot beside a calendar on which ten years had been marked in pencil. A business, she explained, is worth the money it will earn over all those years and not merely the money in this month's drawer, just as a plant is worth the fruit it will give over a long life. A person who judges either one by today's leaves alone will always misjudge its true worth.

Priya told them about a stall near the gate that had once sold a fashionable plastic toy, and that for one summer had been so crowded that the owner had to hire a boy to hold back the queue. The next year the toy was forgotten, the queue evaporated and the stall stood quiet and empty, with unsold toys stacked behind it like a monument. A great month, she said, is not the same thing as a great business, and the difference is time.

On a sheet of squared paper Priya drew two lines side by side, one shooting up like a rocket and then falling back to earth, the other climbing at a slow and almost boring angle. Added up over ten years, she said, the boring line was worth far more than the exciting one, because the area beneath it was so much greater. Ravi saw that the thing which dazzles the eye is rarely the thing which lasts, and he wrote that down too.

Steady profit, Priya continued, gives a business the freedom to think beyond next week. It can hire good people, improve its product, repair its mistakes and survive a bad month without panic, whereas a company living from payment to payment can think only about the next bill. Money earned steadily buys time, and time, in a young company, is the most valuable thing of all.

Nadia pointed out that a good Sunbox should last for many years, which was a quiet blessing for the business as well as for the seller. It meant that customers would come back for repairs and spare parts, and later, when they were happy and growing, for a second or a third box. A product that earns a customer's trust once may go on earning it again every year for a decade.

Priya gave them a single question to ask about any business idea, however exciting it seemed at the moment. Will it still be earning money in ten years, she demanded, and if it will not, what exactly is going to stop it? She had noticed that most founders ask the first half of that question only rarely and the second half almost never, which explained a great deal of failure.

They spent an evening listing everything that could bring the Sunbox's earnings to an end. Rivals might copy the design, cheaper makers might undercut the price, and the idea itself might grow stale as the market and the technology moved on. It was uncomfortable work, rather like inspecting a house for cracks immediately after buying it.

Ravi grew quietly worried as he read the list again, because every item on it pointed in the same direction. If anybody could copy the Sunbox in a month, he said, then the years of steady profit might never arrive, and all their work would merely have shown the market what to build. He lay awake again that night, though this time the problem was his own.

Nadia only laughed at his worried face and said that the answer was simpler than he feared. They must protect the idea, she said, and since protection takes years to build, they had to begin working on it on the very first day, not on the day the copies appeared. Priya nodded so firmly that her pencil fell off the table, and she laughed at herself for being so dramatic.

Priya wrote a short phrase on a card and held it up for the others to read: long-lasting advantage. It meant, she said, whatever it is that stops other people from simply copying a successful product and taking the customers that you won with your own hard work. Without one, a good idea is only a head start, and head starts are short.

Priya drew a castle on the whiteboard, with a high wall, a deep moat and a single narrow gate. A good business needs something like it, she said, a protection that keeps copies out while allowing the right customers to pass through. The drawing was clumsy, but the message was clear enough for anyone who had ever watched a rival arrive.

Ravi tried to imagine a rival buying a Sunbox, laying it open on a bench and copying every part within a week. What, he asked, would stop such a rival from winning the customers away with a lower price and a louder shout? The honest answer, at that moment, was almost nothing, and the three of them stood silent for a while.

Nadia said the first protection was know-how, and she wrote the word in capital letters in her notebook. Anyone could look at a Sunbox and see its parts, she explained, but the patient skill of making all those parts work well together came only from months of learning, failing and learning again. A rival could buy the box in an afternoon but could not buy the experience.

Nadia pointed to the row of failed lids and bent panels on the shelf, each with a label in her handwriting. The seal, the panel angle and the battery had each been born from a mistake, and a copier looking at the finished box would see the answers without ever understanding the questions. Those mistakes, she said with a smile, were the most valuable things in the workshop.

Nadia patiently showed Farid how to fit the seal and how to set the panel at the right angle, and she insisted that he repeat each step aloud. Knowledge that lives only in one person's head, she said, is easily lost, so the whole team would write it down and share it until it belonged to the company and not to any single individual. Know-how, in other words, had to be grown like a garden and not hoarded like a secret.

The second protection, Priya said, was size, and she drew a picture of a factory floor with hundreds of identical boxes stacked in tidy rows. When a company makes a great many boxes, each one costs less than a small maker's, because metal, parts and workers' time are all bought and used more efficiently in large amounts. A rival starting from nothing would find it very hard to match that price without losing money.

Farid showed them a real example from his own work, because he had no patience with theories that could not be proved on a bench. When he ordered a large stack of metal sheets instead of two or three, the price of each sheet fell, and the saving flowed into every box that left the workshop. It was a small difference at first, but small differences, multiplied by thousands, build great walls.

The third protection, Priya said, was trust, and it was the slowest to build and the hardest to copy. A name that sellers rely on keeps its customers loyal, because nobody wants to risk a week's stock on a stranger's box when a familiar one has never let them down. Trust could not be bought in a shop or cut from a sheet of metal; it could only be earned, one kept promise at a time.

A nervous new seller asked Omar whether the Sunbox was really worth buying, and Omar, leaning on his stall with the air of an elder statesman, gave an answer that no advertisement could have improved. The people who made it, he said, always came back when something went wrong, and that was worth more than the metal and the panel put together. Ravi, overhearing from the next stall, had to pretend to be busy with a crate.

Ravi wrote the three protections in his notebook, know-how, size and trust, and drew a small castle beside them for luck. Under them he added a warning for himself, because Priya had reminded him that a wall built around a poor product protects nothing worth keeping. The product must come first and must be truly excellent, she had said, and the walls could be built only on top of that good work.

After weeks of hard work the team stood proudly in front of ten finished Sunboxes, lined up on the workshop floor like soldiers on parade. They delivered them in a borrowed van to ten sellers in the vegetable lane, and each of the three felt the peculiar mixture of pride and terror that comes of sending something you have made out into the world. Whatever happened next, the Sunbox was no longer theirs alone, and its fate now depended on ten ordinary people.

On the first rainy morning a sudden storm swept across Eastgate, drumming on the canvas roofs and sending shoppers running for cover. Water found a thin crack in the lid of one of the Sunboxes and ran inside, where it soaked a whole crate of greens and left a wet patch spreading across the seller's table. By the time Ravi arrived, the seller was standing over the ruined vegetables with a face like thunder.

By noon two more sellers had sent word that their boxes were leaking too, and their messages were not polite. One of them demanded his money back, another threatened to tell the entire market, and the third simply sent a photograph of a puddle with no comment at all. Ravi felt his stomach drop, because it was clear that the fault was not a fluke but a flaw in the design.

Ravi's first instinct was to blame the unusual storm, and perhaps one or two careless sellers who had left their lids open. Priya listened to this speech without interrupting and then told him, gently but firmly, that rain was a normal part of life in a market, and that a box which could not survive it was simply not finished. The comforting excuse dissolved in the face of that plain sentence, and Ravi reached for his notebook instead of his umbrella.

Ravi took an umbrella and a notebook and visited all ten sellers that afternoon, one after another, including the ones whose boxes had never leaked. He told each of them, honestly and without excuses, that the first batch had a fault, and he apologised before asking a single question. He expected anger, but what he met, to his surprise, was a kind of curious respect.

Nadia spent the evening studying the failed lids under the workshop lamp, and at last she found the cause. The rubber seal she had chosen shrank slightly in the hot sun and left a gap at one corner, so that rain could creep in wherever the metal had warmed and moved. She admitted without hesitation that the fault was in her design, and the honesty cost her something, but it also cleared the air.

Nadia designed a firmer seal made of a different kind of rubber, set it into a deeper groove and fitted it to a spare lid. They tested it under a garden hose for a full hour, then in the sun for another, then under the hose again, until Farid declared that a fish could have lived inside the box. Only then did anyone allow themselves to relax, and Nadia celebrated by eating an entire packet of biscuits alone.

Ravi and Nadia went from stall to stall with a bag of new seals and a small toolbox, fitting one to each of the ten boxes without charging a single coin. They replaced even the seals of the boxes that had never leaked, because a problem you know about is a problem you must fix everywhere. The sellers watched with growing interest, as though a doctor had arrived with free medicine.

Priya showed them the cost of the free repairs in a neat column of numbers, and the total at the bottom was painful to read. It had swallowed a good part of their small savings, but she argued that the price was far lower than the price of losing the trust of ten sellers who talked to one another all day. Money spent on honesty, she said, is not a loss but an unusual kind of investment.

In the weeks after the repair, the orders from the lane began to grow, and nobody was more surprised than Ravi. The sellers told one another that these were people who admitted their mistakes and came back to put them right, and in a market full of promises that was a very rare quality. The leak, which had felt like a disaster, had turned out to be the best advertisement they could have hoped for.

A new craze swept through Eastgate like a rumour, and nobody could say where it began. Within a week a dozen sellers in the next lane had painted their stalls bright pink and begun to sell fruit smoothies in elaborate paper cups, and shoppers queued to photograph the drinks on their phones. Everyone agreed that it was the future of the market, and nobody could say exactly why they believed it.

Ravi felt the pull of the crowd and wondered aloud whether the Sunbox company should join in, since so many clever people could not all be wrong. Nadia asked him a sharp question over her tea: were all those sellers right, or were they simply copying one another, each convinced because the others seemed convinced? It is surprisingly hard to tell the difference between the two from the inside of a crowd.

Priya explained how fashion works in business, and she did it with obvious relish. When many people chase the same idea at the same moment, the field becomes crowded, the prices fall and almost nobody earns very much, however fashionable the idea may be. The loudest crowd is often standing exactly where the old problems of competition are waiting.

A month later the smoothie craze faded as quickly as it had arrived, leaving behind a lane of pink stalls like a party that had gone on too long. The sellers were left with fading paint, a stack of cheap blenders and almost no customers, because every shopper had already tried one and every seller had been selling the same cup. Ravi was deeply relieved that the little company had not followed them, and a little proud that it had not.

Ravi took his lesson from the pink lane and wrote it down before he could forget it. The opinion of a crowd, he decided, is not evidence that an idea is good, since a crowd may be right or wrong for reasons unrelated to the facts; sometimes its enthusiasm is itself a warning. Real evidence comes from customers who pay, and from results that can be measured and checked by anyone.

Ravi sat alone at his desk with the notebook under the lamp and practised the difficult art of thinking for himself. He wrote down, in plain sentences, what he believed about the Sunbox, why he believed it and what facts would prove him wrong, because he had noticed that an idea without a test is only a mood. It was uncomfortable work, rather like looking into a mirror in a very strong light.

His first belief was that sellers lose a great deal to heat, and he would be wrong if more careful counting showed the numbers to be small. His second was that a solar box can solve the problem in real markets, and his third was that sellers would pay a fair price for it, month after month and not just once. Beside each belief he wrote what would prove it false, which felt like handing his enemies the sharpest knife in the house.

Ravi circled a date on the calendar, three months ahead, and promised himself that on that day he would check each belief against what had actually happened and not against what he had hoped would happen. A belief that is never tested, he reasoned, will gradually harden into a habit, and habits are very difficult to argue with. He told Priya about the date so that she could remind him if he tried to forget it.

Nadia read the list over his shoulder and, without asking permission, added a line in pencil at the bottom of the page. A hunch, it said, is a perfectly good place to start, but it must never be mistaken for a fact, however many times one repeats it to oneself in the shower. Ravi laughed out loud, and he left her line exactly where it was for the rest of the year.

Mrs Dutta, who had run a corner shop for forty years and trusted nobody's enthusiasm, was invited to explain why she thought the Sunbox would fail. Sellers would be careless, she said, the lids would be left open and thieves would love anything that shone, so the box would vanish within a month of being delivered. Ravi thanked her warmly, added a strong lock to the design and discovered that the most useful people in a project are often the ones who disagree with it politely.

Orders were growing faster than the workshop could fill them, and the team longed to build a hundred boxes in one batch. Priya's calculations showed that the parts, the metal and the wages would cost far more than the small savings they had left after the leaking lids. They would need help from outside, and that meant learning a language none of them had ever spoken.

Priya explained that there are people called investors who give money to a young company in exchange for a small share of its ownership. If the company grows and succeeds, the share becomes worth far more than they paid, and if it fails, they lose what they gave, so they choose carefully. It was an arrangement based on hope and on evidence, in roughly equal measure.

Through a friend of Mrs Dutta, who turned out to know everyone, they were introduced to an investor named Anita Joshi, a calm woman who had helped several small firms through their first difficult years. She agreed to hear a short talk from Ravi the following Friday, together with two colleagues, and she warned him that she disliked long speeches and cared even less for vague ones. Ravi thanked her and then, once the call had ended, forgot how to breathe.

Ravi practised his talk in front of Priya, who held a stopwatch with the expression of a judge at a race. He explained every part, every test, every mistake and every thought that had crossed his mind since the thermometers, and by the time he reached the end the talk had lasted almost ten minutes. Priya said, kindly, that nobody had ever been refused money for being too short.

Together they cut the talk down to three plain sentences, which Priya wrote on a card and pinned above Ravi's desk. The first said what the Sunbox does, the second said exactly who it helps and the third explained why the idea could work now and not ten years ago. Anything that did not serve those three sentences, she told him, belonged in the answers to questions and not in the talk.

Nadia played the part of a tough investor with such enthusiasm that Ravi nearly forgot she was his friend. What if a big company copies you tomorrow, she demanded, and what if the sellers simply stop paying, and why should anyone put money into a box that is made of metal and hope? Ravi answered each question as honestly as he could, and where he did not know the answer he learned to say so.

On Friday morning Ravi stood in front of three seated listeners in a plain office, holding a small Sunbox in both hands like an offering. His fingers trembled, but his voice, to his enormous surprise, was steady, and he began exactly where Priya had taught him to begin, with the bin behind Omar's stall. He told them the three plain sentences from the card, and then, for once in his life, he stopped talking.

The listeners asked many hard questions, some of them sharp enough to draw blood, and Ravi answered each one as honestly as he could. When he did not know something, he said so plainly and explained how he planned to find out, and he noticed that Anita Joshi leaned back and smiled for the first time. Honesty about the limits of what you know, he realised, is more convincing than a confident guess.

Two offers arrived within the week, and one of them was considerably larger than the other, which made it extremely tempting. Priya reminded Ravi that choosing a backer is rather like choosing a companion for a long journey, since both of you must want the same destination and be willing to travel at the same speed. In the end they chose Anita Joshi, who wanted a business that would last, over a larger offer from someone who wanted a quick sale.

Priya read the agreement slowly, line by line, with a pencil in her hand and her lips moving silently, and she asked a friend who knew the law to read it as well. Nobody should sign a paper that they do not fully understand, she said, and an hour of careful reading is cheaper than years of regret. Then, with a feeling like stepping on to a train that has just begun to move, the three of them signed.

With the new money in the bank, the team rented a larger workshop on the same street and hired two assemblers, a quiet young man named Dev and a talkative woman named Salma. Farid closed his old shop next door and joined the company full time, bringing his tools, his forearms and his habit of humming while he worked. The little company had become, almost overnight, a place with a payroll, a timetable and a growing list of people who depended on it.

Every Friday the whole team shared a meal on the workshop floor, sitting on crates and upturned buckets around a long plank laid over two trestles. They laughed, told stories, argued cheerfully about football and passed around Salma's spicy pickles, and gradually the company acquired a character of its own. Nobody had designed it; it had simply grown, the way a good habit grows from repeating one small kindness.

When Ravi interviewed applicants for the next job, he found that he was looking for more than skill. He wanted people who enjoyed the work, who told the truth when something went wrong and who trusted their colleagues with a problem, because a strong small team grows a culture of its own. A single poor hire can spoil that culture for everyone, since skills could be taught in a month but character could not be taught at all.

Ravi wrote a single sentence in thick black letters on a poster and hung it above the workshop door, where everyone would see it each morning. It said that the company existed to help market sellers keep what they grow, and he had rewritten it eleven times before he found words short enough to be remembered. A mission, he had learned, is a promise that you make so often that it begins to shape you.

On early mornings the workers carried boxes out to the van while the sun was still rising, their breath showing in the cool air. The sentence above the door reminded them why the lifting mattered, and because each of them understood the purpose, they pulled in the same direction without being told. A clear mission gives hard work a meaning that wages alone can never supply.

One morning a delivered box turned out to have a scratched panel that would let the sun and the dust in. Ravi might have hoped that the seller would not notice, and the temptation was real, since a replacement would cost a day and a good deal of money. But he thought of the poster above the door and made his decision at once, because a mission is tested not on easy days but on days when the cheap choice is available.

A big trading company, which supplied sellers in half the country, offered to order two thousand boxes in a single month. Ravi's heart jumped, because the chart on his desk would have shot upwards like a rocket, and for a few hours he allowed himself to imagine the headlines. Then Priya laid her hand on the table and asked him, very quietly, what would happen if even a tenth of those boxes had a problem that nobody had yet found.

Ravi thought it over for two nights and saw that growing too fast would spread every small problem across a thousand markets before the team had learned how to solve even one of them. He asked the company for a smaller first order of two hundred boxes, explained his reasons plainly and offered a larger order once the first had proved itself in the field. The company's buyer was surprised, and then impressed, because he had never before met a supplier who asked for less.

Priya reminded the team that food had to be kept safe and that every town had rules about how, which none of them had read. They studied the local regulations with the thoroughness of students before an examination and sent a Sunbox to an independent laboratory, where inspectors measured how well it held its cold and whether the inside stayed clean. It was tedious work, but a rule that protects a customer's dinner deserves respect.

A week later the results arrived in a brown envelope, and the Sunbox had passed every test with room to spare. Priya framed the certificate and hung it beside the mission poster, remarking that rules followed carefully are not a burden but a quiet kind of advertisement, since they give the customer another reason to trust the maker. Ravi, who had once thought of rules as obstacles, began to see them as part of the product.

Once the first lane was truly happy, the team carried the Sunbox to Northfield, a nearby market that looked very much like Eastgate but with a better view of the hills. Omar insisted on coming along, in his best shirt, to tell the Northfield sellers what the box had done for his tomatoes, and his story did more selling in an hour than Ravi's speeches had done in a month. The step was small, and precisely because it was small it succeeded without drama and without any need for heroics.

Ravi set a rule for growth and pinned it to the map: the team would move to the next town only when the last one was working well. Each new step should resemble the one before it, he said, so that the lessons learned in one place could be applied in the next without unpleasant surprises. It was a deliberately patient way to expand, but it was a method that never required them to retreat or to undo their mistakes.

Then came a week of heavy cloud, when the sun scarcely showed its face over Eastgate and Northfield. Some of the Sunboxes could not make enough power to keep up with the cooling, and the vegetables inside them began to warm, to the dismay of sellers who had learned to rely on them. Ravi's phone rang all week with calls that began politely and ended less politely.

Nadia and Ravi leaned over a failing box under a grey sky and decided, after a long and tired argument, to give every future Sunbox a larger battery and a more efficient fan. The change would add a little to the cost and a little to the weight, but it meant that the cold would last through even the dullest week of the year. Every box already sold, Nadia added, would be upgraded free of charge, and nobody at the table was willing to disagree.

One morning a large company called Brightcool launched a copy of the Sunbox from a bright stage with a huge banner and a crowd of cheering guests. It had plenty of money, a famous name and a price that was far lower than Ravi's, and for several hours the three founders sat in the workshop and said almost nothing at all. It was precisely the moment that Priya's list of threats had been written for, and she fetched it from the drawer.

Ravi wanted to panic, but Priya calmly asked him to study the rival's box before doing anything rash, and so they bought one and took it apart on the workbench. It looked remarkably like a Sunbox, down to the colour of the lid, and yet the seal was thin, the panel angle was wrong and the battery was too small for a cloudy week. Brightcool had copied the shape of the answer but not the lessons that had produced it.

A few customers wondered whether to switch to the cheaper box, but most of them stayed, and the reasons they gave were remarkably similar. The Sunbox had proved itself through hot weeks and wet ones, its makers had come back whenever something broke, and nobody wished to gamble a week's stock on a stranger's promise. Trust, it turned out, was a wall that a banner and a low price could not climb.

A few sellers who had switched to the cheaper box found that its lid leaked in the first heavy rain, and they came back to the workshop with an air of polite embarrassment. Ravi welcomed each of them warmly, refrained from saying anything clever and fitted a new Sunbox on the stall before they had finished apologising. Winning, he had decided, is much nicer when nobody has to be humiliated, and the story spread through the lane by evening.

Ravi and Nadia knew that copies would keep coming for as long as the Sunbox was a success, so they refused to rest on the certificate. They sketched an improved model with a lighter body, a stronger lock and a panel that folded flat for travel, and every detail came from a complaint or a suggestion that some seller had made. The best defence against a copier, Nadia said, is to be somewhere else by the time the copy arrives.

In the margin of the shared notebook Priya wrote a sentence that the three of them copied onto their own pages. An advantage is not something you win once and keep for ever, she said, because know-how, size and trust must be earned again every year by the people who hold them. The rival had arrived as a test, and the company, so far, had passed it.

Because the sellers now threw away so much less, they ordered more from the farmers who grew the vegetables, and the trucks that left the farms each morning were fuller than they had ever been. The benefit was spreading in a chain that Ravi had never drawn on any whiteboard, and every link in it was a person with something to gain. Something genuinely new, he thought, rarely helps only the people who buy it, because its benefits spread outward like ripples.

The shoppers gained as well, and they noticed it quickly and without being told by anybody. Even late on a scorching afternoon the lettuces at a Sunbox stall were as crisp as they had been at sunrise, and the tomatoes kept their flavour all the way to the dinner table. A family that buys fresher food, Ravi realised, is a family that has benefited from a stranger's invention without ever knowing his name.

Three busy years passed in a blur of deliveries, repairs and Monday meetings, and the first notebook was almost full. In this imagined story the Sunbox had reached five towns, and about four hundred stalls were using one every day, from the first lane at Eastgate to markets that Ravi had never visited in person. It was not a giant, but it was real, and each of those four hundred stalls had once had a bin behind it that filled up faster than it should.

Omar, the first customer, had become something between a friend and an ambassador, and he travelled to other towns on market days to show new sellers how the Sunbox worked. He told the story of the tomatoes so often that it had acquired a polish, and the sellers listened to him as they would listen to a neighbour, which is exactly what he was. Ravi sometimes thought that Omar had done more for the company than the three founders put together.

Ravi was invited to speak to a class at a small school near the market, and he was more nervous than he had been in front of the investors. He did not talk about money or about company charts, but about a bin behind a stall and a question that had kept him awake one night years before. The children, who had no polite habits to hide behind, listened with their mouths open.

At the end of the talk a small girl in the front row held up a drawing of a strange wheeled machine that would help her grandmother carry water from the well. She asked, with perfect seriousness, whether she was allowed to build it, and the whole class turned to look at Ravi as if he were the person with the answer. He told her that she was not only allowed but needed, and that she should begin by asking her grandmother what she found hardest.

Walking home, Ravi saw that the thinking they had learned was useful far beyond business. In a school, a job, a village or a family, anyone could notice what people had learned to accept, ask whether it had to be so, and try to make something new that was truly useful. The method did not belong to companies, and it did not require a factory.

One evening the three friends sat on the workshop roof with their tea and looked back over the whole journey, from the first sleepless night to the framed certificate by the door. They laughed at how little they had known at the beginning, and then, a little more soberly, at how much they still had to learn. Nobody mentioned success, because it felt too early and too large a word for people who were still learning every week.

Ravi opened a fresh notebook and wrote down, in five short lines, everything that he now believed about making something new. Look for what people have learned to accept, make something much better than what exists, begin with a small market, protect what you build, and keep going when it is hard. Beneath the list he wrote a sentence for himself alone: nothing here is a law, and every point must be tested again.

In short, look closely for the problems that people have stopped noticing, make something markedly better than anything that exists, begin in one modest corner and safeguard what you build. Then keep improving it for as long as it matters to anyone, and let the needs of real people be your guide. This book is general information only, written to help you think about new ideas, and it is not financial advice.
